extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and practitioners handling patent assignments and transfers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal principles governing the effect, scope, and interpretation of assignments/conveyances of patented inventions (including pre‑patent assignments, multiple patents, reissues, extensions, foreign patents, licenses, and rights to past infringements). Useful for drafting, interpreting, and litigating patent assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of 'all rights' warrants a perfect title
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of all rights to the patented invention, in whatever language such rights may be described, transfers or attempts to transfer the entire interest covered by the patent. By it the assignor asserts himself to be the sole owner of the patented invention, free from all incumbrances created by any prior transfer. If the assertion is true the assignee derives an exclusive title; if not true, the assignee takes what the assignor possessed and has a right of action on the implied warranty, or at his option the transfer may be treated as inoperative and void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such language (e.g. 'all the right', 'exclusive right to make and sell ... for the whole term') purports to convey the entire interest and is justified only when the assignor has unqualified ownership of all rights created or protected by the patent. Interpretive cases cited (Pickhardt v. Packard, Nellis v. Pennock Mfg.) illustrate this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of 'all my rights' implies no warranty of title
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of all the rights of the assignor in the patented invention contains no implied averment as to the nature or scope of the interest conveyed. It operates upon any ownership which may be vested in the assignor and transfers it to the assignee subject to any previous conveyances or contracts made by the assignor or predecessors, whether legal or equitable and whether recorded or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignee under this form must be on guard and is chargeable with notice of facts discoverable by inquiry of prior owners or claimants. Cases (e.g. Tumbull v. Weir Plow Co.) show that phrases like 'all my right, title and interest' have been held to convey only the right the assignor then had and not to import a warranty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment transfers only the invention specifically assigned
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a patented invention operates only upon the invention covered by the patent; other inventions owned by the same assignor (modifications, improvements, or independent inventions) are not transferred by the conveyance unless expressly included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if improvements were in existence at time of conveyance or essential to practical use, they are not transferred unless the assignment expressly confers rights in improvements. The assignment of one patented invention does not carry an interest in a different invention (cases: Pnetz v. Bransford, American Hide & Leather v. American Tool & Machine). The elements of separate patents remain distinct in ownership; several patents in one person do not merge into greater rights than the separate patentees had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment affects American patents (original and reissues) but not foreign patents absent express provision
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment will operate upon the original term of the American patent and upon its reissues; but monopolies created by foreign patents are not affected by such transfer except so far as foreign law and an express contractual provision permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor may assign one or more concurrent/successive monopolies (original patent, reissue, extension). Foreign patents create monopolies governed by foreign law; an assignment in the U.S. cannot alone transfer the foreign monopoly — an express clause may create an enforceable contract obligating the assignor to execute necessary foreign conveyances under the foreign law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of assignment upon an extension: extensions are not conveyed unless expressly included
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension (statutory prolongation) is intended for the benefit of the inventor and generally vests in the inventor (or his executor/administrator). The presumption is that an ordinary assignment does not transfer the right to a future extension; an instrument must expressly and unequivocally include the extension to operate upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical assignment language (e.g. 'all my right, title and interest' during 'the term for which a patent may be granted') will usually be construed as limited to the original term and reissues only. To transfer an extension, the assignment must show intent to convey the future interest (cases: Ex parte Holmes; Hendrie v. Sayles). Assignees should insert explicit provisions if they wish to secure monopoly under a possible extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of several patents in one instrument is permissible but clarity is recommended
rubrics_metrics.description: An owner of several patents may assign one, more, or all of them in a single assignment; when each patent is described by date and number the subject matter is clear. A general assignment of 'all such patents as the assignor has in his own right' is valid and transfers patents of which he is apparent owner (but not those held in trust for others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid record confusion, separate conveyances for each patent are desirable. The phrase 'in his own right' excludes patents the assignor holds for others or only in part (cases cited). Trade-marks used with patented articles may be assignable with the patent (Julian v. Hoover Drill Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment does not transfer rights of action for past infringements unless expressly conveyed
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment carries no right to sue for past infringements unless such a right is specifically expressed. Rights to past infringement damages are injuries against former owners and require distinct words of conveyance to transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment of an expired patent may be effective as a power of attorney to collect past damages. Conveyance pendente lite does not affect the litigation; judgments bind parties in accordance with interests involved. Cases cited: Ebonotype Engraving Co. v. Hoke; May v. Juneau Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment revokes revocable licenses and terminates powers of attorney unless assignee recognizes them
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of the entire interest of the assignor in a patented invention revokes all of his revocable licenses and terminates previous powers of attorney, unless the assignee by continuing to recognize them estops himself from denying their validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assignee permits a license or power to remain in force, he may be estopped from denying it. Assignment of an undivided part creates joint ownership and co‑owners' rights are determined by the assignment's provisions; related rights and remedies are treated separately in the treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor's implied warranty of title arises from assignment for valuable consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale/assignment of a patented invention for valuable consideration implies by law a warranty of title to it and of the assignor's right to assign according to the assignment's terms. The warranty arises out of the sale itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express warranties may also be included. The assignee may have remedies against the assignor for breach of implied warranty (cases cited). The warranty does not arise where the assignment language or circumstances show otherwise (see surrounding sections on 'all my rights' vs. absolute grants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee is charged with notice and bound by facts discoverable from prior owners
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee under certain forms of conveyance is put upon inquiry and is chargeable with notice of facts that he might have discovered by inquiring of prior owners or persons claiming rights under the patent; every one who derives title through such an assignment is presumed to have the same knowledge imputed to the original assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language such as 'right, title and interest' may be sufficient to put an assignee on inquiry (cases: Hamilton v. Kingsbury). Recording and supplemental assignments may be construed together; assignee should investigate prior conveyances and claims to avoid taking subject to undisclosed interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of the invention described in the patent includes only that invention and its renewals, not unrelated improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'invention' in an assignment reciting the patent includes only the invention described in the patent and its renewals, not other improvements or distinct inventions, even if the original invention would be less valuable without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments that purportedly convey rights to improvements have been interpreted narrowly; an assignment of rights to 'improvements' must be express to transfer distinct inventions. Cases: United Nickel Co. v. American Nickel Plating Works; Stebbins Hydraulic Elevator Mfg. Co. v. Stebbins. Where parties intended to include future patents or improvements, specific language or separate conveyances are necessary.
